Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
- 30-year-old female nurse with 7 days of persistent fever, sweats, myalgias and nausea 4 weeks after returning from rural Vietnam; high suspicion for malaria or other travel-related infection—requires urgent in-person exam and blood work.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Daily fever with alternating chills/hot sweats for 7 days.
  • Associated: Generalized muscle aches, marked fatigue, nausea, ↓ appetite, night sweats.  
  • Denies: Cough, sore throat, ear pain, diarrhea, urinary symptoms, neck stiffness, new focal headache, rash, joint swelling.
- Past medical history: Chronic mechanical back pain (under physiotherapy); episodic screen/weather-related headaches/migraines.
- Medications: Seroxat (paroxetine); OTC paracetamol & ibuprofen for fever.
- Allergies: Seasonal pollen (hay fever) only.
- Family history: Father died from myocardial infarction at 68 y.
- Social / preventive: Works as a nurse; up-to-date vaccinations incl. Hep B; non-smoker; moderate alcohol; regular moderate exercise.  
  • Travel: Returned from Vietnam 4 weeks ago after trekking/cycling in rural areas, river exposure; took daily malaria prophylaxis (exact drug unknown, possibly dual regimen).

Examination:
- Telephone consult—no direct vitals or physical exam performed.
- Patient reports: No rash, lymph-node swelling, focal joint swelling, or urinary abnormalities.

Impression:
- Most likely: Malaria (fever with hot/cold sweats, myalgias, rural Vietnam exposure, prophylaxis not fully protective).
- Alternative infectious causes:
  • Systemic viral illness (e.g., influenza/COVID-19)—less favored given duration and travel history.  
  • Arboviral infection (dengue/chikungunya) or enteric fever—possible but incubation period and lack of typical features make these less likely.
- Non-infectious causes (e.g., lymphoma) considered only if infection work-up negative.

Plan:
- Arrange same-day face-to-face assessment at central London clinic (or local A&E if easier).  
  • Full physical examination and vital signs.
- Blood tests: 
  • Thick & thin blood films and rapid antigen for malaria.  
  • FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP/ESR, blood cultures, dengue/viral serology as indicated.
- Advise patient not to work until evaluated and cleared.
- Admin team to call patient with appointment; patient to phone provided number within minutes to schedule.
- Provide consult summary to reception if attending A&E.
- Safety-net: If worsening symptoms (rigors, confusion, jaundice, bleeding) before appointment, attend A&E immediately.

Quality checks
● Missing/expected elements: Objective vitals (temp, HR, BP), physical exam findings, current weight, menstrual/Pregnancy status, list of exact malaria prophylaxis agent, vaccination dates, follow-up timing after tests.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear history but lacks objective data; telephone format limits examination; minor conversational noise.
